newsitem.title: USA: U.S. backs 3 permanent council seats for Third World.
newsitem.headline: U.S. backs 3 permanent council seats for Third World.

text.p: The United States, which has long supported making Germany and Japan permanent members of the 15-nation Security Council, said on Thursday it would also back permanent seats for three developing countries.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in Washington that, after a review, "the United States now agrees ... that we ought to have developing countries sit on a permanent basis on the U.N. Security Council as permanent members."
He added: "We believe that the regions themselves -- the African countries, the Latin American countries and the Asian countries -- ought to decide how these seats will be filled."

United States U.N. ambassador Bill Richardson gave details of Washington's new decision to a closed-door meeting of a U.N. working group that has been discussing the issue of council reform for several years. His statement was not immediately made public.

On the question of veto rights, Burns said: "We have not taken a position on the veto for new permanent members including Japan and Germany but we will oppose any resolution which infringes on prerogatives for current permanent members."
The U.S. decision still leaves open a large number of questions that have divided the working group. These include:
- the ultimate size of the council, which now comprises five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- and 10 non-permanent members who each serve two-year terms;
- whether and how many non-permanent members should be added; and
- whether new permanent members should have the power of veto enjoyed by the current permanent five.

Germany and Japan insist they must also have veto rights, while a summit meeting of non-aligned countries in New Dehli earlier this year said any Third World countries that become permanent members of the council must also have a veto.

The United States and some other countries favour limiting an increased council to 21 members, for the sake of efficiency. But others favour an increase to as many as 24 to 26, including up to half a dozen additional non-permanent members.
Italy strongly opposes any increase in the number of permanent council members, as do several countries that fear permanent membership for a regional rival.

How permanent members from developing countries would be chosen is also unresolved. One way would be for individual countries to vie for a seat that they would occupy permanently. Another way would be for permanent seats to be allotted to certain regions, and then rotated among members of that region so that each would fill the seat for a certain number of years.

Any changes in the membership of the Security Council would have to be approved by a two-thirds majority of the 185-member General Assembly and ratified by the parliaments or other constitutional bodies of two thirds of the U.N. membership, including all five current permanent members of the council.

The Council has only once before been increased, from 11 members to 15, by the addition of four non-permanent seats. That was approved by the General Assembly in December 1965 but did not enter into force until June 1968, following parliamentary endorsement.
